Inflation slowed, but prices stayed higher: read the CPI level before resetting your budget

Use five graphics to distinguish Canada’s annual-average CPI level, annual changes, accumulated expense increases and separate hypothetical future price paths.

By TickerLantern Research · Published 25 October 2026 · 5 min read
Sources reviewed 25 October 2026

Historical percentage changes here are calculated from the displayed one-decimal index values, so rounding may differ from published percentage series. Annual averages are not December prices, latest monthly readings or a dated schedule of bills. No income, tax, interest or spending-quantity adjustment is calculated.

The central idea

A smaller positive inflation rate means prices are rising more slowly. It does not erase the increases already embedded in the price level.

01

Ask whether the headline describes a level or a change

A price index and an inflation rate answer different questions. The index records a price level relative to its reference period. A percentage change compares two index levels. When that change becomes smaller but remains positive, the newer level is still higher.

The first two charts use Canada’s all-items annual-average Consumer Price Index from Statistics Canada Table 18-10-0005-01. The dated observations cover 2020–2025 and use the reference 2002=100. The line shows levels; the bars calculate changes from one annual average to the next.

The index rises from 137.0 in 2020 to 164.2 in 2025. The increase from 2024 to 2025 is smaller than the increase from 2021 to 2022, yet 164.2 remains above every earlier annual value shown. A slower pace and a higher endpoint can occur together.

02

Keep the comparison period consistent

Statistics Canada’s 2025 annual review, released 19 January 2026, reports a 2.1% annual-average CPI increase for 2025. It explains that annual-average comparisons differ from the monthly twelve-month change: an annual average combines the twelve monthly index readings, while a monthly comparison uses the same month one year earlier.

These charts therefore do not describe December 2025 prices or the latest monthly inflation rate in 2026. They retain a complete annual period so the levels and changes share a consistent time basis. Six annual points also cannot show every rise and fall that occurred between them.

The change bars are calculated from published index values rounded to one decimal. That rounding can affect a percentage calculated afterward. Use the displayed data tables to inspect the exact source levels and the derived values instead of treating extra decimal places as greater source precision.

03

Calculate the accumulated change from the endpoints

The cumulative index change is 164.2 ÷ 137.0 − 1, or about 19.85%. This compares the 2025 annual-average level with the 2020 annual-average level across five intervals. It does not say that prices increased by that amount in any single year.

Adding the five percentage changes is not the same calculation. Each year’s percentage applies to that year’s starting level. Chaining the growth factors reproduces the ratio of the final index to the initial index because the intermediate index terms cancel.

A zero inflation assumption after 2025 would hold the newer level constant in this simplified example. Returning to the earlier level would require a decline, not merely a smaller positive increase. The size of a decline is measured against the higher starting level, so it is not numerically equal to the earlier cumulative rise.

04

Translate an index ratio into a clearly labelled budget illustration

Enter a hypothetical monthly expense expressed in 2020 dollars. The default CAD 3,000 is scaled by each annual index divided by 137.0. At the 2025 index, the result is about CAD 3,595.62. This assumes the expense moves exactly with the all-items CPI and that the underlying quantity or standard of consumption stays comparable.

The waterfall starts with CAD 3,000 and adds the changes in that monthly expense equivalent. Its endpoint is a new monthly level. The intervening steps are not a total of the bills paid during the five years; calculating actual historical spending would require the amounts and frequency of those bills.

An individual budget can change differently because of its spending mix, contracts, location or choices. The entered amount is not an observed Canadian household average, and the index ratio does not calculate your personal inflation rate. Use the separate spending-basket guide when comparing how categories affect your own expense mix.

05

Separate future assumptions from the historical evidence

The future line starts at the CPI-scaled 2025 expense and applies two user-selected annual changes. The default 2% followed by 1% produces 1.02 × 1.01 − 1 = 3.02% cumulative growth. The monthly expense equivalent becomes about CAD 3,704.21 after the two hypothetical years.

The flat comparator applies zero change in both years and stays at CAD 3,595.62. It does not fall back to CAD 3,000. That comparison shows why a return to low inflation would not, by itself, restore an older household budget.

Try a negative future change to illustrate a declining price level. The fixed matrix gives other two-year combinations independently of the controls. A 2% increase followed by a 2% decrease gives 1.02 × 0.98 − 1, or minus 0.04%, rather than exactly zero. These scenarios illustrate arithmetic; they assign no probability to future inflation.

06

Update the dollar budget using the level you actually face

For a household decision, start with current bill amounts and the dates they become payable. A dated CPI comparison can explain accumulated price pressure, but it does not replace a quote for rent, an insurance renewal or a grocery budget based on what the household buys.

Keep the amount, comparison period and unit beside every number. An index value of 164.2 is neither CAD 164.20 nor a 164.2% annual inflation rate. A 2.1% annual-average change is not automatically the rate on every category or every family’s bill.

When testing the next budget, label the future changes as assumptions and revise them when bills become known. The planning question is how many dollars the household will need and when, even when the headline percentage looks smaller than before.
